spanish-0.introTitle: Give the three sentences different jobs
opening: Soy estudiante means I’m a student. Estoy en la biblioteca means I’m in the library. English uses I’m twice; Spanish chooses a different verb for these two jobs.
Start by saying who you are, where you are, and what you have: Soy estudiante. Estoy en la biblioteca. Tengo una pregunta. We’ll build the three sentences below.
spanish-0.remember: Soy estudiante identifies you; estoy en la biblioteca locates you; tengo una pregunta says what you have.
spanish-0.reasoningTitle: Why the English I am is not enough to choose the verb

spanish-5.introTitle: You are allowed to stop and ask again
opening: The café worker says ¿Para aquí o para llevar? You miss it. Say ¿Puede repetirlo más despacio, por favor?—Can you repeat it more slowly, please?
When you hear the choice, para aquí is for here and para llevar is to go. We’ll listen to the exchange and hear how a short clarification keeps it moving.
spanish-5.remember: Ask for repetition when you miss the sound; ask ¿Qué significa…? when you need the meaning.
spanish-5.reasoningTitle: Find the choice inside the question

spanish-6.introTitle: Ask for one place, then check the turn
opening: ¿Dónde está la farmacia? asks where the pharmacy is. You can ask that without knowing every word the answer might contain.
Listen for recto, straight ahead; derecha, right; and izquierda, left. If you are unsure which turn you heard, repeat that part as a question before walking away.
spanish-6.remember: Recto is straight ahead, derecha is right, and izquierda is left. Repeat the turn as a question if you need it checked.
spanish-6.reasoningTitle: What the directions are telling you to do

spanish-7.introTitle: Keep the coffee; change the day
opening: Your friend asks ¿Quieres tomar un café el sábado? You like the idea but cannot Saturday. Say Me gustaría, pero no puedo el sábado.
Now offer the day that works: ¿El domingo? We’ll finish the exchange by settling a time, rather than leaving both people with different plans.
spanish-7.remember: Separate wanting to meet from being available. Agree on the day and the time.
spanish-7.reasoningTitle: Which part of the invitation are you accepting?

piano-0.introTitle: Count the beats while the sound continues
opening: Tap four even beats: 1, 2, 3, 4. Now hold one sound across 1 and 2. You kept two beats but began only one note.
We’ll stay on C and compare four short notes with two held notes. Keeping the pitch the same makes the rhythm easier to hear.
piano-0.remember: A two-beat note begins once and lasts through two beats. It does not ask for two presses.
piano-0.reasoningTitle: The beat keeps going underneath a held note

piano-4.introTitle: Find three notes before sounding them together
opening: Start on C, skip D to E, then skip F to G. C–E–G is a C-major chord.
Hear C, E and G one at a time first. Then hear the same notes together. The pitches have not changed; only the timing of their beginnings has.
piano-4.remember: C–E–G makes C major. Separately is an arpeggio; together is a block chord.
piano-4.reasoningTitle: Why these three notes make this chord

piano-5.introTitle: Let the left hand stay while the right hand moves
opening: Give the left hand one low C to hold. The right hand will play E–D–C–D over it, one note on each beat.
Listen to each part separately, then hear them together. The difficult moment is often beat 2: the right hand changes, but the left must keep holding.
piano-5.remember: One held bass note can sit under four changing melody notes. The hands have different jobs.
piano-5.reasoningTitle: Put the two jobs together slowly

piano-6.introTitle: Find both chord shapes before adding a clock
opening: C major is C–E–G. The F-major shape here is F–A–C, farther to the right. Try finding each shape without worrying about speed.
Then give C four beats, F four beats, and C four more. We’ll slow the change down so the hand can arrive without making the beat rush.
piano-6.remember: C–E–G to F–A–C is a hand movement as well as a change of sound. Learn the arrival before speeding it up.
piano-6.reasoningTitle: Make the movement fit an even count

chess-0.introTitle: Read a square, then trace the move
opening: A square name gives its column first and row second. D4 is on the d-file and fourth rank. With White at the bottom, files run a to h from left to right.
Choose a piece in the diagram. A rook goes straight, a bishop goes diagonally, and a king goes one square. The knight uses a two-and-one jump. These are movement diagrams, not complete games.
chess-0.remember: A movement shape is only part of a legal move. In a game, inspect blockers, the destination and your king’s safety too.
chess-0.reasoningTitle: The route depends on the piece

chess-3.introTitle: Look from the knight’s new square
opening: White’s knight can jump from e5 to f7. From f7 it attacks Black’s king on h8 and rook on d8 at the same time.
The king attack is check, so Black must answer it first. We’ll move the king to a safe square, then take the rook. Use the board to follow every move.
chess-3.remember: Verify both targets from the fork square, then inspect the opponent’s reply.
chess-3.reasoningTitle: Why the check gives White time

chess-4.introTitle: Look at the move after the capture
opening: A bishop on c4 has a clear diagonal to a knight on f7. It can take the knight—but can Black take the bishop afterward?
We’ll play the capture twice, changing only Black’s king position. That one change turns a free knight into a possible exchange.
chess-4.remember: A clear capture path does not tell you whether a capture is free. Check the opponent’s reply.
chess-4.reasoningTitle: The same capture can have a different reply

chess-5.introTitle: Open a path and put a piece on it
opening: On the starting board, White’s bishop on f1 is blocked by its own pawns. Playing e4 clears e2, opening a diagonal for that bishop.
We’ll develop the knights and bishops while watching what each side attacks. There is a reason behind each move; you do not have to memorize the line as unexplained letters.
chess-5.remember: Name the job of your move, then look at what the opponent changed. An opening is a conversation between both sides.
chess-5.reasoningTitle: Connect the pawn moves to the piece moves
